title: Bad Estimates from a Local Variable: OPTION (RECOMPILE)
description: A local-variable 'unknown' estimate picks a scan a real value wouldn't; OPTION(RECOMPILE) lets the optimizer see the value and seek. Why it matters: parameter sniffing is one of the most notorious, hard-to-diagnose SQL Server performance issues in production -- the same stored procedure can be instant for one caller and catastrophic for another.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine asking a tailor to make you a suit, but instead of measuring you, they measure some other random person who happened to be standing nearby, and then cut your suit to that person's size. If that other person happens to be about your size, you get lucky and it fits fine. If they're a foot taller than you, the suit is a disaster — and it has nothing to do with the tailor's skill, only with the fact that they measured the wrong person. This lesson is about SQL Server doing something conceptually similar: building a query plan based on the wrong "measurement" of how much data to expect.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** When SQL Server compiles a query that references a parameter or variable, it needs to guess how many rows will match, in order to choose a good execution plan (the same estimating problem you've already seen in other lessons — it decides between things like index seeks and full scans based on expected row counts). Ordinarily, when you use a real parameter (like in a stored procedure), SQL Server is smart enough to "sniff" the actual value being passed in on first execution and build statistics-based estimates specific to that literal value — this is usually a good thing, and is where the term "parameter sniffing" comes from. This lesson focuses on a related but distinct trap: when a query instead uses a local variable that gets assigned a value inside the batch, SQL Server deliberately does *not* peek at that variable's actual value during optimization, because the value could still change later in the same batch. Instead, it falls back to a generic, "typical value" guess for the whole column — and that generic guess can be wildly wrong for the specific value actually used at runtime.

**Why this happens in real databases.** This pattern shows up constantly because it looks completely reasonable to write — declaring a local variable, assigning it a value, and then filtering with it feels no different from using a parameter directly. But SQL Server's optimizer treats the two very differently under the hood, precisely because a local variable's value is, from the optimizer's point of view, not knowable at compile time in the same trustworthy way a passed-in parameter's value is.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** When you filter using a real parameter — say a stored procedure parameter `@CustomerId` used directly in a `WHERE` clause — SQL Server looks at the actual value passed in for the very first execution, consults the column's statistics for that specific value, and estimates "how many rows actually have this value" accurately. But when you instead write `DECLARE @V INT = @CustomerId; ... WHERE Column = @V`, the optimizer treats `@V` as an "unknown at compile time" quantity, on the theory that a local variable's contents aren't fixed the way an incoming parameter's are. Rather than sniffing its actual value, the optimizer falls back to a density-based guess — essentially "assume an average, typical number of rows per distinct value across the whole column," regardless of what `@V` actually equals. If the real value you're filtering on is unusually common (matches far more rows than the "average" value would) or unusually rare (matches far fewer), that generic guess is simply wrong for this specific execution, in either direction. Built on that wrong guess, the optimizer might choose an index seek plan meant for a small, rare value when actually thousands of rows match, causing thousands of expensive, unnecessary lookups — or choose a full scan meant for a common value when actually almost nothing matches, needlessly reading a huge table for a handful of rows.

**Why this matters in production.** This is one of the most notorious and hardest-to-diagnose performance problems in SQL Server, precisely because the query looks completely fine, uses no obviously bad syntax, and the "wrong" plan was arrived at through a perfectly logical (if misapplied) optimizer safeguard. It's especially confusing because the same query text can perform brilliantly for some values and catastrophically for others, with nothing in the code distinguishing the two cases — the only variable is which value happens to be in play at that moment, something you can't tell just by reading the query. The fix demonstrated in this lesson is `OPTION (RECOMPILE)`, a query hint that tells SQL Server "don't reuse a cached, generic plan — recompile this query fresh every time, using the actual current values of any local variables involved." That forces the optimizer to build a plan tailored to the real value in play for this specific execution, restoring the accurate, value-specific estimate a genuine parameter would have gotten in the first place — at the cost of recompiling the query every single time it runs, which is a real trade-off worth understanding rather than a free win.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below runs the same query shape with a local variable holding first a common value and then a rare one, and shows you that both executions reuse the exact same generic, one-size-fits-all plan regardless of which value is actually in play. After adding `OPTION (RECOMPILE)`, re-run both cases and watch each one get its own tailored plan, built around the actual value used in that specific execution — a direct, visible illustration of the difference between a plan built for "some typical value" and a plan built for the value that's actually there.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** This lesson focuses on the local-variable variant specifically, but the closely related, more famous version of parameter sniffing happens even with genuine stored-procedure parameters: SQL Server caches the very first plan compiled for a procedure and reuses it for every subsequent call, so if the first call happened to use an unusually rare or unusually common value, every later call — even with a completely different, more typical value — gets stuck with a plan optimized for that first, possibly atypical, execution. `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` fixes both variants the same way, at the cost of recompiling every time; other tools like plan guides or query hints targeting a specific "typical" value exist for cases where recompiling on every call is too expensive to accept.

## Scenario
`DECLARE @s VARCHAR(12) = 'Open'; SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE Status = @s;` returns only ~200 rows (the `Status` values are heavily skewed), yet the plan is a full **Clustered Index Scan** of all 300,000 rows.

## Why it's slow
The value lives in a **local variable**. At compile time SQL Server cannot see what `@s` holds, so instead of using the histogram it falls back to the **density vector** — the *average* rows-per-value across all statuses (~100,000). Believing 100,000 rows will match, it decides the non-covering `IX_Orders_Status` seek would trigger 100,000 key lookups and rejects it, scanning the whole table instead. This is the same estimation trap as classic **parameter sniffing**: the plan is built for a guessed cardinality, not the real one.

## What to look for
- A **Clustered Index Scan** even though the predicate is highly selective.
- Reads far larger than the handful of rows returned — the estimate, not reality, drove the plan.

## The concept
Add `OPTION (RECOMPILE)`. It recompiles at execution time and **embeds the literal value** of `@s`, so the optimizer probes the histogram for `'Open'` specifically, estimates ~200 rows, and switches to an **Index Seek** with a key lookup. `RECOMPILE` trades a little extra CPU per run for an accurate, value-specific plan — ideal for queries over skewed data.
startingQuery: DECLARE @s VARCHAR(12) = 'Open'; SELECT OrderId, CustomerId, OrderDate, Total FROM Orders WHERE Status = @s;
hints: The value is in a local variable, so the optimizer can't sniff it and uses the average (density) estimate instead of the histogram.
That average estimate (~100k rows) is wildly wrong for the rare 'Open' status, so it scans instead of seeking.
Add OPTION (RECOMPILE) so SQL Server recompiles with the actual value embedded and re-estimates from the histogram.
